# The Widow’s Guide

> Eight practical books for women in the United States in the first two years after a husband dies, by Edward Crowe (JMS Media Group LLC). Each chapter answers one question with a short answer first, then what to do, what can wait, and who can help. Rules, phone numbers and web addresses were checked against the agencies’ own pages in October 2026. General information, not legal, financial, tax, medical or mental-health advice.

## Start here

- [The eight books](https://widowsguide.org/books/): which book covers which stretch of time
- [Every question in the books](https://widowsguide.org/questions/): all 96 chapter questions
- [Words you will hear](https://widowsguide.org/words/): glossary of benefit, estate, tax and housing terms
- [Widow, widower, widowed](https://widowsguide.org/widow-or-widower/): what each word means, and why agencies say surviving spouse
- [How to tell Social Security someone has died](https://widowsguide.org/telling-social-security/): who reports it, what to have ready, and the payment for the month of death
- [Who to notify when your husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/who-to-notify-when-someone-dies/): six calls for the first week, ten for the first month, what can wait, and a letter for many of them
- [Social Security widow’s benefits](https://widowsguide.org/widow-social-security/): when she can start, how much (71.5% to 100%), how long it lasts, working, remarriage and how to apply
- [What happens to a joint bank account when a spouse dies](https://widowsguide.org/joint-bank-account-after-death/): survivorship, tenants in common, payable on death, deposit insurance, and what to ask the bank
- [Am I responsible for my husband’s debts?](https://widowsguide.org/husbands-debts-after-death/): generally not; the four exceptions, community property states, credit cards, medical bills, Medicaid and collectors
- [Survivor benefits after a husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/survivor-benefits/): Social Security, pensions, OPM, the military Survivor Benefit Plan and the VA
- [What a widow is entitled to when her husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/what-a-widow-gets/): Social Security, the $255 payment, pensions, insurance, joint property, health coverage and debts, in one place
- [Does a surviving spouse need probate?](https://widowsguide.org/does-a-spouse-need-probate/): what passes without it, small-estate processes, and the executor
- [Filing taxes after your husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/taxes-after-husband-dies/): joint return, qualifying surviving spouse, the house, Medicare premiums (SSA-44) and free tax help
- [What happens to the house when your husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/house-after-husband-dies/): the deed, probate, the mortgage, a reverse mortgage and taxes
- [Transferring a car title after your husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/car-title-after-death/): the motor vehicle office and short heir forms
- [VA and military benefits for widows](https://widowsguide.org/military-survivor-benefits/): the Survivor Benefit Plan through DFAS, VA DIC, the Survivors Pension, CHAMPVA, burial, and what remarriage changes
- [The Social Security death benefit](https://widowsguide.org/social-security-death-benefit/): the one-time $255 payment, who can get it, the two-year deadline, and other money paid at a death
- [Letters to send after your husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/letters/): free templates for a credit bureau, creditors, his bank, a life insurer, his employer, his pension plan, utilities and a debt collector, each with what to enclose and what the answer means
- [What widows and families search for when a husband dies](https://widowsguide.org/what-widows-search/): 5,819 Google autocomplete searches from 30 October 2026, grouped by topic, with a free CSV (CC BY 4.0)
- [What to say to a widow](https://widowsguide.org/what-to-say/): what helps, what lands badly, and the offers that get used
- [The First Two Weeks checklist (PDF)](https://widowsguide.org/assets/the-first-two-weeks.pdf)
- [If today is very bad](https://widowsguide.org/help-tonight/): 988, the Veterans Crisis Line and other help
- [About the books](https://widowsguide.org/about/): how they are written and how facts are checked

## Book 1: The First 30 Days (The first month)

What to Do, Who to Call, and What Can Wait After Your Husband Dies. Who to call, what to find, what can wait. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/)

- [Where do I even start?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/where-do-i-even-start/): Start with this week, not with everything. Almost nothing has to happen today. A handful of things have to happen this week, and most of what people mention can wait a month or more.
- [Who can help me with all this?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/who-can-help-me-with-all-this/): Choose one person to be your second pair of hands, and give everyone else a specific job. People who offer usually mean it. They are waiting to be told what.
- [What happens with the funeral home?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/what-happens-with-the-funeral-home/): You can take this more slowly than it feels. The law lets you see the prices before you choose, and you do not have to decide everything at one meeting.
- [How many death certificates do I need?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/how-many-death-certificates-do-i-need/): More than you think. Banks, insurers, pension plans and government offices each want a certified copy, and many of them keep it. A few extra now is easier than ordering more later.
- [What has to happen this week?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/what-has-to-happen-this-week/): Six calls. The funeral home may already have done part of one or two of them, such as telling Social Security, and some will not apply to you.
- [What about everyone else I'm supposed to call?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/what-about-everyone-else-im-supposed-to-call/): No. About thirty calls can wait weeks or months, and some never need making. Here they are, sorted by when.
- [Where are the papers?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/where-are-the-papers/): Most of what you need is in a handful of usual places, and almost all of it can be replaced if it is not there. Start one folder now and fill it as things turn up.
- [Is there a will, and what do I do with it?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/is-there-a-will-and-what-do-i-do-with-it/): Not this week, in most cases. Keep the original safe, hand nothing out yet, and book a first meeting with a probate or estate lawyer this month.
- [Which bills do I keep paying, and which do I stop?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/which-bills-do-i-keep-paying-and-which-do-i-stop/): Keep paying the bills that keep the house running, including the mortgage and any car loan. Hold off on any other debt in his name until you have asked whether you owe it.
- [How do I keep the house, and myself, safe right now?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/how-do-i-keep-the-house-and-myself-safe-right-now/): For the next few months, treat anything urgent that involves money as a scam until you have checked it. Checking is usually one step: hang up, and call back on a number you look up yourself.
- [Why can't I think straight?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/why-cant-i-think-straight/): No. Some widows describe not being able to think, remember or decide in the first weeks. While it lasts, write everything down and decide as little as you can.
- [What can wait, and for how long?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-30-days/what-can-wait-and-for-how-long/): No. Almost everything people urge you to decide in the first month can wait. The few things with real deadlines are already in this book. Everything else can wait until you can think.

## Book 2: The Money (Months 1 to 6)

Survivor Benefits, Accounts, and Insurance After Your Husband Dies. Survivor benefits, accounts, insurance. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/)

- [Where do I stand right now?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/where-do-i-stand-right-now/): Before any decision, make one page: what income stopped, what continues, what may start, what you own, what you owe, and what you don't know yet.
- [What happens with Social Security?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-happens-with-social-security/): It may be one of several. Survivor benefits depend on his work record, your age when you start, and your own benefit. Sometimes you can take one benefit first and switch to the other later.
- [Will his pension keep paying, and what about his service?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/will-his-pension-keep-paying-and-what-about-his-service/): It depends on a choice made when his pension started, and that choice usually cannot be changed now. The plan can tell you exactly what was chosen and what, if anything, you will receive.
- [What do I do with his retirement accounts?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-do-i-do-with-his-retirement-accounts/): Usually not right away, but the choice is hard to reverse. A surviving spouse often has more than one way to receive these accounts.
- [How do I claim the life insurance?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/how-do-i-claim-the-life-insurance/): You don't have to pick in a hurry. Claiming is usually simple: a form and a certified copy of the death certificate.
- [What happens to our bank accounts?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-happens-to-our-bank-accounts/): Usually yes, for an account in both your names. How each account was set up decides what happens to it. Most joint accounts pass to you, though not all.
- [Do I have to pay his debts?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/do-i-have-to-pay-his-debts/): You're generally not responsible for his debts. They are paid from his estate, and if the estate can't pay, the debt usually goes unpaid. There are four exceptions.
- [What happens to the house and the car?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-happens-to-the-house-and-the-car/): Generally, not just because he died. Federal law generally stops a lender from calling the whole mortgage due because he died.
- [Will I still have health insurance?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/will-i-still-have-health-insurance/): Maybe not for long. Coverage through his job can end, and the ways to keep or replace it have time limits. Find out this week exactly when yours ends and what your options are.
- [What changes with taxes this year?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-changes-with-taxes-this-year/): More than usual, but not all at once. There will be a final return for his part of the year, and you can usually still file jointly for the year he died.
- [What should I not decide yet?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/what-should-i-not-decide-yet/): Very little of it is urgent. A few things have real deadlines, and this chapter puts them in one list, each with the chapter that explains it.
- [Who can I trust to help with money?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-money/who-can-i-trust-to-help-with-money/): Look for someone you pay directly, not someone paid by what they sell you, who will promise in writing to act in your interest at all times. Different questions need different people.

## Book 3: The House and the Things (Months 3 to 12)

Deciding Whether to Stay, and Clearing a Life, After Your Husband Dies. Stay or sell, and clearing a life. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/)

- [Do I have to decide about the house now?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/do-i-have-to-decide-about-the-house-now/): Probably not this year. A few situations do set a clock. They are money that will not stretch, a reverse mortgage, a rented home, a house you cannot safely manage, or other people with a share in it.
- [What if I want to move right away?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/what-if-i-want-to-move-right-away/): Sometimes it is, and some widows who moved in the first year were glad they did.
- [Can I afford to stay?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/can-i-afford-to-stay/): You can find out, and the answer may be less frightening on paper than it is in your head.
- [Can I manage the house on my own?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/can-i-manage-the-house-on-my-own/): Perhaps with help, and help can be hired. List what the house needs each season, and mark what you can do, what you can hire, and what worries you. The worries tell you more than the list does.
- [If I moved, where would I go?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/if-i-moved-where-would-i-go/): There are more choices than staying where you are or moving near a child. Each one costs you something different, whether that is money, the friends around you, or some of your independence.
- [Whose decision is it?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/whose-decision-is-it/): You do. Other people can have views, and some may have a legal share if the house was not fully yours. Where you live is still your decision. You can listen to them without agreeing.
- [When should I start on his things?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/when-should-i-start-on-his-things/): No. There is no right time to start on his things. Some widows start within weeks because seeing his things hurts, and others wait years because seeing them helps. Either way is ordinary.
- [How do I clear his things without clearing him out?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/how-do-i-clear-his-things-without-clearing-him-out/): You can keep the things that hold him without keeping everything he owned. Work in one small area at a time, and sort what you find into five boxes.
- [Who should get what?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/who-should-get-what/): Start with what the will says, if anything. For the rest, ask each person privately what matters to them before anyone takes anything, and use a fair way to choose when two people want the same thing.
- [What do I do when someone takes something?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/what-do-i-do-when-someone-takes-something/): First find out whose it was: the estate's, yours, or already theirs. Then decide which things matter enough to ask for back.
- [What is it all worth, and how do I sell it?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/what-is-it-all-worth-and-how-do-i-sell-it/): Most household things are worth less than it feels they should be, and a few are worth more than anyone guesses. You can't always tell which is which by looking.
- [What about everything nobody wants?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-house-and-the-things/what-about-everything-nobody-wants/): Donate what someone can use, recycle what you can, and pay someone to haul away the rest. You can do it in that order, and usually over as many weeks as you like.

## Book 4: Everything They Handled (Months 1 to 9)

The Practical Things That Are Now Yours After Your Husband Dies. The practical jobs that are now yours. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/)

- [What did he actually do around here?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/what-did-he-actually-do-around-here/): Probably more than either of you ever wrote down. In many long marriages the work gets divided without a list, and each of you stops seeing the other's half.
- [How do I find every account he had?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/how-do-i-find-every-account-he-had/): Follow the money. Twelve months of bank and card statements show almost every bill, subscription and account that was paid for. His mail and his tax forms show most of the rest.
- [How do I get into his phone, computer and email?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/how-do-i-get-into-his-phone-computer-and-email/): There are proper ways in, and they are slower than guessing.
- [How do I keep track of the bills?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/how-do-i-keep-track-of-the-bills/): One list, one calendar, one place to pay. Start with the master list from How do I find every account he had?.
- [How do I look after the car?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/how-do-i-look-after-the-car/): The owner's manual has the car's schedule, and a mechanic you trust can help you keep to it. The title, the registration and the insurance need your name on them. That is most of it.
- [What does the house need, and when?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/what-does-the-house-need-and-when/): A house has a short list of things to know and a longer list of things to do each season. You can learn the short list in one afternoon with someone who knows houses.
- [Learn it, hire it, or leave it?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/learn-it-hire-it-or-leave-it/): Neither, as a rule. Decide each job on its own: how often it comes, how hard and risky it is, what it costs to hire, and whether you want to learn it.
- [How do I hire someone without being taken advantage of?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/how-do-i-hire-someone-without-being-taken-advantage-of/): Check them, compare them, and pay in stages. Find people through someone you trust, check their license if your state issues one, confirm their insurance, and get written prices from more than one.
- [Who is trying to scam me?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/who-is-trying-to-scam-me/): Treat any call, text or knock you didn't expect as not real until you have checked it yourself. Details in an obituary can lead scammers to you. Grief makes anyone easier to rush.
- [What about the paperwork he did every year?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/what-about-the-paperwork-he-did-every-year/): The yearly paperwork comes around on a calendar. Taxes, insurance renewals, Medicare choices and property tax each arrive at roughly the same time every year.
- [What if I was the one who handled everything?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/what-if-i-was-the-one-who-handled-everything/): Because he may have done things nobody would call jobs: the company in the evening, the driving at night, the heavy lifting, the calls to his side of the family.
- [What if something happens to me?](https://widowsguide.org/books/everything-they-handled/what-if-something-happens-to-me/): You can leave the person after you the list you may have needed yourself. Write down where everything is, put your own legal papers in order with a lawyer, and tell one person where to look.

## Book 5: The First Year (Months 6 to 15)

Anniversaries, Holidays, and the Hardest Months After Your Husband Dies. Anniversaries, holidays, the hardest months. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/)

- [Why can month six feel lonelier than month one?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/why-can-month-six-feel-lonelier-than-month-one/): Nothing is wrong with you. In the first months people came, the phone rang, and there was a great deal to do.
- [What do I do with the evenings and weekends?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/what-do-i-do-with-the-evenings-and-weekends/): Give them a shape. The hours the two of you shared can be the hardest, because nothing fills them on its own. A few fixed points, decided ahead, can carry you further than willpower will.
- [Is what I'm feeling normal?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/is-what-im-feeling-normal/): The feelings in this chapter are ones widows describe. The health website MedlinePlus calls grieving “part of the normal process of reacting to a loss.
- [How do I get through his birthday, our anniversary, and the day he died?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/how-do-i-get-through-his-birthday-our-anniversary-and-the-day-he-died/): The days before a date like this can be harder than the day itself. You do not have to get through it on willpower alone. Decide ahead what you will do.
- [What do I do about the holidays?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/what-do-i-do-about-the-holidays/): You are allowed to change the rules this year. You can host or not, go away, skip it, or keep it exactly as it was. Whatever you choose, decide early and tell your family plainly.
- [Why can't I sleep, and why don't I eat?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/why-cant-i-sleep-and-why-dont-i-eat/): Health agencies name changes in sleep and appetite among the things you may notice after a loss. Both are worth mentioning to your doctor if they go on, or if they worry you.
- [Should I talk to my doctor about this?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/should-i-talk-to-my-doctor-about-this/): Yes, and before you need to. Tell your doctor that he died, and mention any change in your sleep, eating, drinking or mood. You do not have to work out whether something is grief or something more.
- [What about the days that have no reason?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/what-about-the-days-that-have-no-reason/): Those days can come without warning, even when nothing has happened. You can have a short list ready for them. Write it on a good day, and it tells you what to do on a bad one.
- [Shouldn't I be better by now?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/shouldnt-i-be-better-by-now/): There is no deadline. The timelines other people hand you can say more about their own comfort than about your grief. Feeling steadier can come early or much later, and either is ordinary.
- [What do I do about the headstone and the ashes?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/what-do-i-do-about-the-headstone-and-the-ashes/): Nothing in a hurry. No federal rule sets any time limit for keeping ashes at home. Keeping them is a matter of state law, and it is generally allowed.
- [Would a grief group or counselor help?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/would-a-grief-group-or-counselor-help/): For some people, yes, and there is more than one kind. A group, a counselor and an online community work in different ways, so not liking groups rules out only one of them.
- [What happens when the year is over?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-first-year/what-happens-when-the-year-is-over/): The first anniversary of his death can be a hard day, and it is not a finish line.

## Book 6: The People Around You (Months 3 to 18)

Family, Friends, and Who Disappears After Your Husband Dies. Family, friends, and who disappears. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/)

- [Why are people acting so strangely around me?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/why-are-people-acting-so-strangely-around-me/): Probably nothing you did. Some people are so frightened of saying the wrong thing to a widow that they say nothing at all. Keeping their distance can be the easiest way to do that.
- [Why do people say such terrible things?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/why-do-people-say-such-terrible-things/): People who say these things may be trying to make it better, without knowing how. You do not have to accept what they say, or answer it.
- [Why have our couple friends drifted away?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/why-have-our-couple-friends-drifted-away/): It may not mean they stopped caring. Couple friendships can run on couples: dinners for four, his friends and their spouses, your friends and theirs, an even number at the table.
- [How do I keep the friends worth keeping?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/how-do-i-keep-the-friends-worth-keeping/): You can go first: a specific plan, on a specific day, and a plain sentence that you still want them in your life. People who are unsure may need an invitation more than they need time.
- [How do I help my children while they grieve too?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/how-do-i-help-my-children-while-they-grieve-too/): You can't grieve for them, and you don't have to fix their grief. You can tell them they don't need to protect you, and let each of them grieve in their own way.
- [How do I talk to my children about money?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/how-do-i-talk-to-my-children-about-money/): You decide what they know. It can help to tell your children that there is a plan, even without the details, and to keep your own accounts in your own control. Gifts and loans can wait.
- [How do I talk to my children about the house?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/how-do-i-talk-to-my-children-about-the-house/): Have the conversation once, with everyone. Start by telling them what you have decided about deciding: when the decision will be made, and by whom.
- [What do I tell my children about me?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/what-do-i-tell-my-children-about-me/): Tell them who you are now: what you need from them, what you don't, and how you are actually doing. They may be guessing. Guessing can make people hover, or stay away.
- [What about his family, and his children from before?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/what-about-his-family-and-his-children-from-before/): His family may be grieving too, and grief and money together can bring out hard feelings in anyone. You can't control how they grieve, and you don't have to settle it for them.
- [Where do I find other widows?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/where-do-i-find-other-widows/): Other widows are in grief groups, faith communities, senior centers, widows' organizations and online, and perhaps on your own street. They can understand without being told.
- [How do I make new friends at this age?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/how-do-i-make-new-friends-at-this-age/): Much the same way as at any age. You see the same people again and again, and one day you are the one who suggests coffee. It can take longer than it used to, and the first months can feel awkward.
- [What about being alone?](https://widowsguide.org/books/the-people-around-you/what-about-being-alone/): Being alone and being lonely are different things, and you may come to like the first.

## Book 7: Year Two (Months 15 to 24)

Rebuilding a Life That Is Yours After Your Husband Dies. Rebuilding a life that is yours. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/)

- [Why does the second year feel so strange?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/why-does-the-second-year-feel-so-strange/): The second year can feel like this. The sharp grief can soften, many of the tasks may be done, and other people may think you are fine. What is left can be quieter and harder to name.
- [Who am I, if I'm not his wife?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/who-am-i-if-im-not-his-wife/): You are still the person who was in that marriage. You are also someone you may not have met for a long time.
- [Do I keep wearing the ring?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/do-i-keep-wearing-the-ring/): Wear it, move it, put it away, or have it made into something else. None of these is a statement about how much you loved him, and none has a deadline.
- [Whose house is it now?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/whose-house-is-it-now/): It is your home, and you are allowed to make it look that way. Changing a room does not erase him. He is in what you remember and what you choose to keep, wherever the sofa sits.
- [What do I actually want?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/what-do-i-actually-want/): You don't have to know yet. You can start small, and notice what catches your attention. Wanting can come back slowly, often in small things first.
- [Should I go back to work, or start something?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/should-i-go-back-to-work-or-start-something/): It isn't silly. Work can bring money, a shape to the week, or company, and it can also mean starting something of your own.
- [Would volunteering help?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/would-volunteering-help/): It can, if you find something that suits you. There is a lot more to choose from than hairnets. Volunteering can bring back a role and a shape to the week, and it can put new people around you.
- [Can I travel on my own?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/can-i-travel-on-my-own/): Yes, you can, and some widows do. You can start with a short trip and choose the way of traveling that suits you: alone, with a friend, or in a group. Some moments may be hard.
- [Should I move somewhere new?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/should-i-move-somewhere-new/): Neither, necessarily. A move in the second year can be a move toward something you want, and not only away from the grief.
- [Why do I feel guilty for feeling better?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/why-do-i-feel-guilty-for-feeling-better/): Some widows describe exactly this. Guilt can come with a good day, because feeling better can feel like leaving him behind. It isn't leaving him. Love doesn't need you to keep suffering to prove it.
- [How do I keep him with me?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/how-do-i-keep-him-with-me/): You don't have to choose between him and a new life. Some widows keep their husbands with them through stories, rituals and things done in his name. A new life can hold him.
- [What do I want the next ten years to look like?](https://widowsguide.org/books/year-two/what-do-i-want-the-next-ten-years-to-look-like/): When you're ready, yes. A single page is enough. It needs one line each for where you'll live, who you'll see, what you'll do, what the money allows, and what your papers say.

## Book 8: Someone New (Month 18 and after)

Companionship, Family, and Money After Your Husband Dies. Companionship after loss, and what people may say. [About the book](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/)

- [Is it too soon to want someone?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/is-it-too-soon-to-want-someone/): No. There is no right time to want company, and wanting it again is not a betrayal of him. Some widows are surprised to want someone again, sometimes after saying they never would.
- [What do I actually want: a friend, a companion, or more?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/what-do-i-actually-want-a-friend-a-companion-or-more/): Yes, it is a thing. Friendship, companionship and dating are three different things, and naming which one you want changes where you look, what you say, and what you agree to.
- [Where do people my age meet someone?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/where-do-people-my-age-meet-someone/): In much the same places people meet friends. Some meet through people they already know, some through something they do every week, and some online.
- [How do I date after forty years?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/how-do-i-date-after-forty-years/): Nerves make sense. It has been a long time, and Saturday matters to you. Some things about dating have changed since you last did it, and some have not.
- [How do I stay safe online?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/how-do-i-stay-safe-online/): Stop before you send anything. A request for money from someone you have not met in person is the mark of a romance scam, however real he seems.
- [What about being close to someone again?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/what-about-being-close-to-someone-again/): Go at your own pace, and say out loud what that pace is. Holding hands, a kiss, a night together: each one can wait until you want it, and you can want one without the others.
- [What will my children say?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/what-will-my-children-say/): What a grown child says can be a fear in disguise. “It's too soon” can mean they are afraid their father will be forgotten.
- [How do I tell my children?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/how-do-i-tell-my-children/): If you have no children, much of this chapter won't apply to you. His family, your friends and everyone else are in What will everyone else think?
- [What will everyone else think?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/what-will-everyone-else-think/): Some people may judge, and some may surprise you. You don't owe anyone an explanation for wanting company again. It can help to have one short, calm sentence ready before anyone asks.
- [If it gets serious, what happens to the money?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/if-it-gets-serious-what-happens-to-the-money/): It depends on the benefit, and for some of them on your age on the day you marry. Some survivor benefits continue after a remarriage at a certain age, and some stop.
- [What happens to the house and the will?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/what-happens-to-the-house-and-the-will/): It depends on how you set things up, and on the law where you live. If you live together without marrying, a partner is generally not one of your heirs.
- [Can I love someone new and still love him?](https://widowsguide.org/books/someone-new/can-i-love-someone-new-and-still-love-him/): Yes. You can love someone new and still love your husband, and neither love has to shrink to make room for the other.
